doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

chapter: Growing up with jazz in northern England
title: Other singers and understanding Bessie Smith's lyrics
summary: She admired Ethel Waters and Eva Taylor for diction; discusses unfamiliar phrases in Bessie's lyrics, John Hammond's music, and Bessie's non-Gospel voice.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens

blocks.x: Who was the next vocalist to effect you like Bessie Smith did?

Nobody ever really effected me like Bessie, but I was cognizant of other singers and one was Ethel Waters of course. I admired enormously Ethel Waters because she had great diction. If you’ll understand that I couldn’t understand what Ma Rainey was saying, and I had trouble with Bessie, I found that with Ethel Waters she had beautiful diction. And then of course Eva Taylor, I loved Eva Taylor’s singing. Because Eva had a great sort of clarity to her voice. So I was impressed by these singers. I didn’t turn on to Billie Holiday until much, much later in life.

Was there a language, not a barrier but some of the things that Bessie Smith may have sung, even if you understood what she was saying, that there was a new phrase in there that maybe wasn’t common to English.

Yeah, we were not hip to a lot of these things, and certainly even today. John Hammond was very kind to me and he gave me quite a lot of music of Bessie’s. And I was pleased to see in some of the written words, the words that I’d been singing, lyrics I’d been singing, that everybody sort of who’d been singing. You know a lot of the singers who sing the Bessie Smith material had been singing incorrect words. Just sort of you made them up as an educated guess. But there are certainly words that were indigenous not to the north of England, and I felt a bit corny, a bit of a fake singing them, because I didn’t have any frame of reference for singing that. And I didn’t know about “my man done gone left me” and so on, and I didn’t know about the “achin’ head” because I was too young to have had a “achin’ head.” But I knew she was saying something that was reaching me. And it was an unusual voice. And Bessie had great purity in her voice. I’m not talking about the last record she made, I’m talking about the first record she made with the Bessemer Singers. She had almost a holy voice but she was not a Gospel singer. I want to make that point right up front. Today’s singers that want to sing like Bessie always introduce Gospel. Bessie was not. She didn’t have any Gospel in her voice at all. I’m adamant about that.
